question: Two thirds of a number N is 24. What is three quarters of N?
hint: First find the whole number. How much is one third of it?
solution: Two thirds are 24, so one third is 12 and the whole number is 36. One quarter of 36 is 9, so three quarters are 27.

A.text: 18 is three quarters of 24, as if 24 were the whole number. It is only two thirds of it.

B.text: 36 is the whole number, found on the way; the question asks for three quarters of it.

D.text: 16 takes two thirds of 24, but 24 already is the two thirds, so the number is bigger than 24, not smaller.

E.text: 9 is one quarter of the number; three quarters are three times as much.

question: A pack holds 24 crayons. Ben takes a quarter of the pack, and Lucy takes a third of the whole pack. How many crayons are left in the pack?
hint: Work out each child's share of the full pack before taking anything away.
solution: A quarter of 24 is 6 and a third of 24 is 8. Together they take 6 + 8 = 14 crayons, so 24 - 14 = 10 are left.

B.text: 14 is how many crayons Ben and Lucy take, not how many are left.

C.text: 12 takes Lucy's third from the 18 crayons Ben left, but she takes a third of the whole pack.

D.text: 18 takes away only Ben's quarter; Lucy's crayons still have to come out.

E.text: 17 is 24 - 4 - 3: the 4 and the 3 of a quarter and a third were taken away as crayons instead of dividing 24 by them.

question: Tom writes the fractions 1/12, 2/12, 3/12 and so on, up to 12/12. How many of them are bigger than 1/3 but smaller than 3/4?
hint: How many twelfths make one third, and how many make three quarters?
solution: A third of 12 is 4, so 1/3 is 4/12, and three quarters of 12 is 9, so 3/4 is 9/12. Between them lie 5/12, 6/12, 7/12 and 8/12, which makes 4 fractions.

A.text: 6 also counts 4/12 and 9/12, but they are equal to 1/3 and 3/4, not bigger or smaller.

B.text: 5 is 9 - 4, which counts one of the two ends as well.

C.text: 2 counts only 5/12 and 7/12. 6/12 and 8/12 count too, even though they can be written as 1/2 and 2/3.

D.text: 8 keeps only one of the two limits: 1/12 to 8/12 are all smaller than 3/4, but the first four are not bigger than 1/3.

question: Oleg spends half of his coins on a book. Then he spends a quarter of the coins he has left on a pen. Now he has 30 coins. How many coins did he have at first?
hint: Work backwards. The 30 coins are what part of the coins he had after the book?
solution: After the pen he keeps three quarters of what he had, and that is 30 coins. So a quarter is 10, and he had 40 coins after the book. Those 40 are half of his coins, so at first he had 80.

A.text: 40 is what he had after buying the book; the half he spent on it still has to be added back.

C.text: 120 takes the pen's quarter of all his coins, but it was a quarter of the coins he had left.

D.text: 50 is how many coins he spent on the book and the pen together.

E.text: 60 only doubles the 30 and forgets the pen, which he bought after the book.

question: A jug full of juice weighs 1500 g, jug and juice together. When only 1/3 of the juice is left in it, the jug weighs 700 g. How many grams of juice does the full jug hold?
hint: What does the difference between 1500 g and 700 g weigh?
solution: The difference, 1500 - 700 = 800 g, is the juice that was drunk, and that is 2/3 of the juice. So 1/3 of the juice weighs 400 g, and all of it weighs 1200 g.

A.text: 300 g is the empty jug, not the juice.

B.text: 800 g is only the two thirds that were drunk; one more third is still in the jug.

C.text: 1500 g is the jug and the juice together, and the jug itself is part of that weight.

E.text: 400 g is the juice still left in the jug, a third of all the juice.

question: In a car park, 5/8 of the cars are red and the rest are blue. There are 6 more red cars than blue cars. How many cars are in the car park?
hint: What fraction of the cars are blue, and how big is the gap between the two fractions?
solution: The blue cars are 3/8 of all the cars, so there are 5/8 - 3/8 = 2/8 of the cars more red ones. That 2/8 is 6 cars, so 1/8 is 3 cars, and there are 8 × 3 = 24 cars: 15 red and 9 blue.

B.text: 15 is the number of red cars, only part of the car park.

C.text: 9 is the number of blue cars, not all the cars.

D.text: 16 takes the 6 as the number of blue cars, but 6 is how many more red cars there are.

E.text: 6 is the gap between the red and the blue cars, copied from the question.

question: In a library, 2/5 of the books are novels. Half of the novels and 1/6 of the other books have hard covers. What fraction of all the books have hard covers?
hint: Pick a number of books that splits into fifths and into sixths, and count.
solution: Take 30 books: 12 are novels and 18 are other books. Half of the novels is 6 and a sixth of the others is 3, so 9 of the 30 books have hard covers, which is 9/30 = 3/10.

A.text: 2/3 adds 1/2 and 1/6, but those are shares of the novels and of the other books, not of the whole library.

B.text: 1/5 counts only the hard-cover novels and leaves out the other books.

D.text: 7/10 is the share of books with soft covers.

E.text: 1/12 multiplies 1/2 by 1/6, but the two groups of hard-cover books have to be added.

question: A box holds more than 20 but fewer than 40 sweets. Exactly 1/3 of them are toffees and exactly 3/8 are mints, and the rest are chocolates. How many chocolates are in the box?
hint: For which numbers of sweets are a third and three eighths both whole numbers?
solution: A third and three eighths of the sweets must both be whole, so their number divides by 3 and by 8, that is, by 24. Between 20 and 40 only 24 does. Then there are 8 toffees and 9 mints, which leaves 24 - 8 - 9 = 7 chocolates.

A.text: 24 is the whole box; the chocolates are only part of it.

B.text: 17 is the toffees and the mints together, not the chocolates.

C.text: The limits 20 and 40 settle it: only a box of 24 lets a third and three eighths both be whole.

D.text: 7/24 is the share of chocolates; the question asks how many there are.

question: Five friends share a pizza. The first eats half of it. Then each of the others in turn eats part of what is left: the second 1/3 of it, the third 1/4, the fourth 1/5 and the fifth 1/6. What fraction of the pizza is left?
hint: After the first friend, half of the pizza is left. How much is left after the second?
solution: Cut the pizza into 60 equal slices. The first eats 30 and leaves 30. The second eats 10 and leaves 20, the third eats 5 and leaves 15, the fourth eats 3 and leaves 12, and the fifth eats 2 and leaves 10. So 10 of the 60 slices are left, which is 1/6.

A.text: 1/5 is what is left after only four friends; the fifth still eats 1/6 of that, which leaves 1/6 of the pizza.

C.text: 5/6 is the part of the pizza the friends ate, not the part that is left.

D.text: Taking every share of the whole pizza, 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/5 + 1/6 is more than 1. But each share is of what is left, so some pizza always remains.

E.text: 1/30 is how much of the pizza the fifth friend eats, not how much is left.
